module_title: Sourcing and Identifying Lemongrass, Eucalyptus, and Tea Tree

lessons.title: Where to Find Lemongrass in Local Markets and Farms
lessons.body: Lemongrass (Cymbopogon citratus) grows wild in many parts of Africa, but for oil production you need a reliable source. Start by visiting local markets that sell fresh herbs and traditional medicine. In countries like Kenya, Nigeria, Ghana, and South Africa, lemongrass is often sold in bunches by women who harvest from their gardens. Ask vendors where they get it â they may connect you to farmers. A single mature lemongrass clump can yield 200-300 leaves per harvest, and you can harvest 3-4 times per year. Look for thick, pale green stalks with a strong lemon smell when crushed. Avoid stalks that are yellowing or dry. If you want to grow your own, lemongrass propagates easily from stalks: cut the bottom 5 cm of a fresh stalk, place it in water for 1-2 weeks until roots appear, then plant in well-drained soil. It needs 6-8 hours of sunlight daily and 800-1500 mm of rainfall per year. In drier areas, irrigate weekly. You can also find lemongrass at large farms that supply supermarkets or herbal processors. Contact agricultural extension officers or farmer cooperatives in your district â they often know who grows it commercially. In West Africa, check with ministries of agriculture for lists of registered herb farmers. When buying from farms, ask for the harvest date. Freshly harvested lemongrass (within 2-3 days) gives the highest oil yield. If you must store it, keep it in a cool, shaded area and use within 5 days. For oil extraction, you need about 100 kg of fresh leaves to produce 0.5-1 kg of oil, depending on the variety and distillation method. So secure a steady supply before investing in a still.

lessons.title: Identifying Eucalyptus Trees in Your Area and Harvesting Leaves
lessons.body: Eucalyptus trees are common in many African countries, especially in South Africa, Kenya, Ethiopia, and Zimbabwe. They are tall (often 20-40 meters), with smooth, peeling bark and long, narrow leaves that hang downwards. The leaves are leathery, grey-green, and have a strong medicinal smell when crushed. To confirm you have eucalyptus, look for the distinctive operculum (a cap) on the flower buds, and the woody seed capsules that look like small cups. The most common species for oil production are Eucalyptus globulus (blue gum) and Eucalyptus citriodora (lemon-scented gum). E. globulus has a camphor-like smell, while E. citriodora smells like lemon. For oil extraction, harvest mature leaves from the lower branches â these have higher oil content than young leaves. The best time to harvest is during the dry season when oil concentration is highest. Use a sharp pair of pruning shears or a sickle to cut branches, then strip the leaves by hand. Wear gloves because the oil can irritate skin. A single mature tree can yield 20-50 kg of leaves per harvest, and you can harvest every 6-12 months without killing the tree. Never cut the main trunk â only side branches. After harvesting, spread leaves in a thin layer in a shaded, well-ventilated area to dry for 2-3 days. This reduces moisture and prevents mould. You need about 50-100 kg of fresh leaves to produce 1 kg of eucalyptus oil. If you donât have trees on your land, ask local forestry departments or tea estates â they often have eucalyptus plantations and may sell leaves. In Kenya, for example, the Kenya Forestry Research Institute (KEFRI) can advise on sustainable harvesting. Always get permission before harvesting from public or private land.

lessons.title: Tea Tree: How to Recognize and Source It in Africa
lessons.body: Tea tree (Melaleuca alternifolia) is native to Australia, but it is now grown in several African countries, including South Africa, Kenya, Zimbabwe, and Zambia. It is a small tree or shrub (up to 6 meters) with narrow, needle-like leaves and papery, layered bark. The leaves are soft, aromatic, and have a strong medicinal, camphor-like smell. Tea tree grows best in warm, humid areas with 800-1200 mm annual rainfall and well-drained, acidic soil. It cannot tolerate frost. If you are in a high-altitude region, you may need to grow it in a greenhouse or under shade cloth. To source tea tree, contact commercial essential oil farms in South Africa (e.g., in Mpumalanga or KwaZulu-Natal) or Kenya (e.g., around Mount Kenya). Some nurseries sell tea tree seedlings. You can also propagate from cuttings: take 10-15 cm semi-hardwood cuttings, dip in rooting hormone, and plant in a mist bed. Roots form in 4-6 weeks. For oil production, harvest the leafy tips (top 30 cm of branches) when the plant is 12-18 months old. Harvest in the morning after dew has dried. You need about 100-200 kg of fresh leaves to produce 1 kg of tea tree oil. After harvest, distill immediately or dry in a shaded, well-ventilated area for 2-3 days. Tea tree oil is prone to oxidation, so use fresh material. If you cannot find tea tree locally, you can substitute with other Melaleuca species that grow in Africa, such as Melaleuca quinquenervia (broad-leaved paperbark), but the oil composition differs. Always test a small batch before large-scale production. For sourcing, join farmer groups on Facebook or WhatsApp â many African essential oil producers share leads on where to buy seedlings and leaves.

lessons.title: Buying Dried Herbs vs. Fresh for Oil Extraction
lessons.body: When extracting essential oils, you can use either fresh or dried plant material, but each has trade-offs. Fresh herbs generally give higher oil yield and better aroma because volatile compounds havenât evaporated. For lemongrass, fresh leaves yield about 0.5-1% oil by weight, while dried leaves yield 0.3-0.7%. For eucalyptus, fresh leaves yield 1-2% oil, dried leaves 0.5-1%. For tea tree, fresh leaves yield 1-2% oil, dried leaves 0.5-1.5%. However, fresh material is bulky and perishable. You must distill within 2-3 days of harvest, or the leaves will ferment and lose oil. Dried herbs are easier to store and transport. You can dry them in a shaded, well-ventilated area for 3-7 days until they are brittle but still green. Never dry in direct sunlight â that destroys oils. A simple test: bend a leaf; if it snaps, itâs dry enough. Dried herbs can be stored in burlap sacks in a cool, dark room for up to 6 months. But beware: dried herbs absorb moisture and can grow mould. Check for musty smell or black spots. For small-scale producers, fresh is better if you have a still nearby. For larger operations, drying allows you to collect material over time and run the still continuously. Cost-wise, fresh herbs are cheaper per kg because they contain water, but you need more weight. For example, to get 1 kg of lemongrass oil, you need about 100-200 kg fresh leaves or 150-300 kg dried leaves. Calculate your transport and storage costs. In Africa, many farmers sell fresh herbs at markets. If you buy dried, ensure it was dried properly â ask the seller how. Avoid herbs that are brown, dusty, or smell weak. Always buy from a trusted source and test a small batch before committing to a large order.

lessons.title: Working with Local Farmers to Secure Steady Supply
lessons.body: To run a successful essential oil business, you need a reliable supply of raw material. Working with local farmers is the best way to ensure this. Start by identifying farmers who already grow lemongrass, eucalyptus, or tea tree in your area. Visit their farms, see their practices, and discuss your needs. Be clear about quantity, quality, and timing. For example, if you need 500 kg of fresh lemongrass per week, tell them. Offer a fair price â check local market rates and add a small premium for consistent quality. A written contract, even a simple one, protects both sides. Include: crop type, quantity, harvest date, price per kg, payment terms, and quality standards (e.g., no mould, no pesticides). Train farmers on proper harvesting and post-harvest handling. Show them how to cut lemongrass at the base, how to strip eucalyptus leaves without damaging trees, and how to dry herbs in shade. Provide tools if needed â pruning shears, sacks, or drying racks. Many farmers will appreciate this because it reduces waste and increases their income. Consider forming a cooperative or farmer group. This allows you to aggregate supply from many smallholders and negotiate better transport rates. In Kenya, for example, the Tea Tree Growers Association helps members access markets. You can also offer advance payments or loans for seeds and seedlings. This builds loyalty and ensures they prioritize your order. Plan for seasonality: lemongrass grows year-round in tropical areas but slows in dry seasons. Eucalyptus leaves are best in dry season. Tea tree harvests peak in summer. So diversify your sources â have at least three farmers for each crop. Keep records of each farmerâs performance: yield, quality, timeliness. Pay on time, every time. Trust is your most valuable asset. With a steady supply, you can focus on distillation and marketing.

lessons.title: Checking Quality: How to Tell Good Raw Material from Bad
lessons.body: Quality raw material is the foundation of good essential oil. Whether you buy fresh or dried herbs, you must inspect them before distillation. Hereâs how. For lemongrass: look for bright green, firm stalks. The leaves should be long and slender, with a strong lemon scent when crushed. Avoid stalks that are yellow, brown, or slimy. Check for mould â a grey or white fuzz. Smell the cut end: it should be intensely lemony, not musty. For eucalyptus: leaves should be grey-green, leathery, and unbroken. Crush a leaf â it should release a strong camphor or lemon smell. Avoid leaves with black spots, holes (insect damage), or a dull colour. For tea tree: leaves should be dark green, needle-like, and aromatic. Avoid leaves that are dry and brittle (unless you are buying dried) or have a weak smell. Moisture content matters. Fresh herbs should be turgid (not wilted). Dried herbs should be brittle but not powder-dry. A simple test: take a handful and squeeze. If it feels damp or sticks together, itâs too wet and will mould. If it crumbles to dust, itâs too dry and has lost oil. Aim for 10-15% moisture for dried herbs. You can buy a cheap moisture meter (around $20) or use the salt test: mix a sample with dry salt; if salt clumps, moisture is high. Also check for contaminants: soil, stones, insects, or other plants. A good supplier will sort and clean. Ask for a sample before buying in bulk. Distill a small batch (e.g., 1 kg) and measure oil yield. If yield is below expected (e.g., less than 0.3% for lemongrass), reject the lot. Finally, trust your nose. Good raw material smells clean, fresh, and true to the plant. Bad material smells mouldy, fermented, or chemical. Never distill bad material â it wastes time and fuel, and the oil will be poor quality.

quiz.q: What is the best way to identify lemongrass in a local market?
options: A) Look for thick, pale green stalks with a strong lemon smell
B) Look for thin, purple stems with no smell
C) Look for broad, round leaves with a minty smell
D) Look for dried, brown roots
quiz.explanation: Lemongrass has thick, pale green stalks and a strong lemon aroma when crushed.

quiz.q: How many times per year can you harvest a mature lemongrass clump?
options: D) Never, it dies after one harvest
quiz.explanation: A mature lemongrass clump can be harvested 3-4 times per year.

quiz.q: What is the ideal way to propagate lemongrass?
options: C) From the bottom 5 cm of a fresh stalk placed in water
quiz.explanation: Lemongrass propagates easily from the bottom 5 cm of a fresh stalk placed in water until roots appear.

quiz.q: How much fresh lemongrass leaves are needed to produce about 1 kg of oil?
quiz.explanation: About 100-200 kg of fresh lemongrass leaves yield 1 kg of oil.

quiz.q: Which eucalyptus species smells like lemon?
quiz.explanation: Eucalyptus citriodora is known as lemon-scented gum.

quiz.q: What part of the eucalyptus tree should you harvest for oil?
options: C) Mature leaves from lower branches
quiz.explanation: Mature leaves from lower branches have higher oil content.

quiz.q: How often can you harvest leaves from a mature eucalyptus tree without killing it?
quiz.explanation: You can harvest every 6-12 months if you only cut side branches.

quiz.q: What is the best time to harvest eucalyptus leaves for highest oil content?
quiz.explanation: Oil concentration is highest during the dry season.

quiz.q: How much fresh eucalyptus leaves are needed to produce 1 kg of oil?
quiz.explanation: About 50-100 kg of fresh eucalyptus leaves yield 1 kg of oil.

quiz.q: What is a key characteristic of tea tree leaves?
options: B) Narrow and needle-like with a medicinal smell
quiz.explanation: Tea tree leaves are narrow, needle-like, and aromatic.

quiz.q: Which climate is best for growing tea tree?
options: B) Warm and humid with well-drained soil
quiz.explanation: Tea tree grows best in warm, humid areas with well-drained, acidic soil.

quiz.q: How can you propagate tea tree if you cannot find seedlings?
quiz.explanation: Tea tree can be propagated from 10-15 cm semi-hardwood cuttings.

quiz.q: When is the best time to harvest tea tree for oil?
options: A) When the plant is 12-18 months old
B) When it is 5 years old
quiz.explanation: Harvest leafy tips when the plant is 12-18 months old.

quiz.q: How much fresh tea tree leaves are needed to produce 1 kg of oil?
quiz.explanation: About 100-200 kg of fresh tea tree leaves yield 1 kg of oil.

quiz.q: What is a disadvantage of using fresh herbs for oil extraction?
quiz.explanation: Fresh herbs are bulky and must be distilled within 2-3 days.

quiz.q: What is the recommended moisture content for dried herbs before distillation?
quiz.explanation: Aim for 10-15% moisture for dried herbs to prevent mould and preserve oil.

quiz.q: How can you test if dried herbs are dry enough?
quiz.explanation: Dried herbs should be brittle and snap when bent.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid drying herbs in direct sunlight?
options: A) It makes them too dry
quiz.explanation: Direct sunlight destroys the volatile oils in herbs.

quiz.q: What is a simple test for high moisture in dried herbs?
options: A) Mix with salt; if salt clumps, moisture is high
B) Add water; if it floats, moisture is high
C) Smell it; if it smells sweet, moisture is high
D) Weigh it; if heavy, moisture is high
quiz.explanation: The salt test: if salt clumps when mixed with herbs, moisture is high.

quiz.q: What should you do before buying a large batch of raw material?
options: A) Distill a small sample to check oil yield
quiz.explanation: Always distill a small sample to verify oil yield and quality.

quiz.q: What is a key benefit of working with local farmers?
options: B) Steady supply of raw material
C) Less need for quality checks
quiz.explanation: Working with local farmers ensures a steady supply of raw material.

quiz.q: What should a simple contract with a farmer include?
options: B) Crop type, quantity, harvest date, price, payment terms, quality standards
quiz.explanation: A written contract should specify all key terms to protect both parties.

quiz.q: Why is it important to train farmers on post-harvest handling?
options: B) To reduce waste and improve quality
quiz.explanation: Proper handling reduces waste and maintains oil quality.

quiz.q: How many farmers should you have for each crop to ensure steady supply?
options: D) None, you can grow your own
quiz.explanation: Having at least three farmers per crop diversifies risk and ensures supply.

quiz.q: What is a good practice when paying farmers?
options: A) Pay late to keep cash flow
B) Pay on time, every time
C) Pay only after selling oil
D) Negotiate lower price after harvest
quiz.explanation: Paying on time builds trust and loyalty.

quiz.q: What should you check for in fresh lemongrass?
options: B) Bright green, firm stalks with strong lemon smell
quiz.explanation: Good lemongrass is bright green, firm, and strongly aromatic.

quiz.q: What does a musty smell in dried herbs indicate?
quiz.explanation: A musty smell indicates mould or poor storage conditions.

quiz.q: What is a sign of insect damage in eucalyptus leaves?
quiz.explanation: Holes in leaves are a sign of insect damage.

quiz.q: Why should you never distill bad raw material?
options: A) It wastes time and fuel and yields poor oil
quiz.explanation: Bad material wastes resources and produces low-quality oil.

quiz.q: What is a cheap tool to check moisture content of herbs?
quiz.explanation: A moisture meter (around $20) can measure moisture content.
